transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Nice to meet you. Well, honestly, it took me a while to actually make this appointment because I kept telling myself it wasn't a big deal, but... what really made me finally come in is what's been happening at work lately. I'm an advertising sales agent, and it's a really dynamic job, which I usually love, but we have these huge, sprawling sales strategy meetings. I mean, they block out hours for these things, and we're all crammed into the main conference room going over quarterly projections and client pitches. 

And the thing is, I know I’m supposed to just stay seated and look attentive like everyone else on the team, but I just... I keep getting up. I really can't help it. It's like this physical itch I have to scratch. I'll find absolutely any excuse to leave my chair, even if it’s just to refill my water bottle for the third time in an hour, or sometimes I'll just go stand and pace by the printer in the corner like I'm waiting for a document that doesn't even exist. My coworkers are starting to give me these looks, and I just feel so unprofessional because I'm thirty years old and I should be able to sit through a strategy session without needing to wander around the room. It’s just so frustrating because I want to stay put, I really do, and I tell myself beforehand that I'm going to just sit there, but my body is just like, "nope, time to move," and then I'm out of my seat again before I even consciously decide to do it.
Do you also have trouble paying attention or staying focused?

Oh, definitely. Yes. It's actually a huge problem, and it kind of ties into the whole meeting thing I was just talking about. Like, I’ll be in those same strategy meetings, right? And I go in with the best intentions. I’ve got my notebook out, my favorite pen, I’ve had my coffee, and I’m looking right at the presenter. I’m thinking, "Okay, we are going to nail these quarterly projections." And for the first few minutes, I’m totally locked in. I’m following the numbers, I’m nodding along. 

But then... it’s like someone just unplugs a cord in my brain. I won’t even realize it’s happening at first. I’ll just suddenly snap back to reality and realize I’ve been staring at the exact same PowerPoint slide—like, maybe a graph about Q3 ad spend—for what feels like ten minutes, and I have absolutely zero idea what the person at the front of the room just said. Nothing. It’s a complete blank. 

And it’s not just in meetings, either. It happens when I’m by myself at my desk, trying to read through a new client brief. These briefs are so important, you know? They have all the details about what the client wants for their campaign, their target demographics, their brand voice, all of that. I’ll start reading, and I’m reading the words, but after a paragraph or two, I realize I’m just moving my eyes across the page. I’m not absorbing a single thing. I’ll have to go back and re-read the same paragraph three, four, maybe five times before it actually sticks in my head. It’s exhausting, honestly. I feel like I’m working twice as hard just to keep up with the basic information everyone else seems to just absorb on the first try. It’s like my brain just decides it’s done paying attention, even when I really, really need it to.
Did these attention and restlessness problems start before you were 12 years old?

Oh, wow, yeah. Absolutely. I mean, I remember this starting way, way before high school. Actually, it’s funny you ask about being younger than twelve, because my mom used to keep all my old report cards and teacher evaluations in this big binder, and every single parent-teacher conference in elementary school was pretty much the exact same conversation. 

They would always write these notes saying that I was a really bright kid, which, you know, is nice to hear, but then there was always a "but." It was always, "she’s bright, but she rushes through everything." And the talking! I was constantly getting in trouble for talking out of turn. I just couldn't seem to hold my thoughts in—if the teacher asked a question, I’d just blurt out the answer before she even finished calling on someone else, or I'd be chatting with the kid next to me when we were supposed to be doing silent reading. 

And the homework situation was a constant battle. I was always forgetting my homework. Half the time I’d actually do it at home, but then I’d leave it on the kitchen counter, or I'd forget to even write down what the assignment was in the first place. And my desk... oh my gosh, my desk in like, third and fourth grade was a complete disaster zone. If you lifted the top, it was just stuffed to the absolute brim with half-finished papers, crumpled up worksheets, old permission slips... just a total mess. It was like a black hole in there. My teachers would literally have to make me stay inside during recess sometimes just to empty the whole thing out on the floor and sort through it because things were just getting lost in the abyss. 

So, yeah, when I think about it, this isn't really a new thing at all. It's just... it's just the adult version of it now, I guess. Instead of a desk stuffed with half-finished coloring pages, it's my email inbox and my client briefs, which is why it feels so much more stressful and embarrassing now that I'm supposed to be a professional. But the feeling itself? Yeah, that's been there since I was a little kid.
Do you often interrupt other people before they finish speaking?

Oh, god, yes. All the time. It’s actually one of the things I’m most self-conscious about, especially in my line of work where communication is literally everything. Like, I’ll be in a pitch or even just a casual catch-up with a client, and they’ll start asking a question—and my brain just immediately races ahead. I’ll think I know exactly where they’re going with it, so I just... I often just jump right in with an answer before a client or a coworker has even finished asking the question. 

And it’s so embarrassing because half the time, they finish their thought while I’m talking over them, and I realize I answered the completely wrong thing, or I just totally cut them off and derailed their whole point. 

Like, just last week, my manager was trying to ask me about the timeline for a digital campaign, and she goes, "For the new social push, are we thinking—" and I just instantly blurted out, "Yes, the graphics are done!" And she just stared at me, took this long breath, and said, "...are we thinking of launching on Tuesday or Wednesday?" I just wanted the floor to swallow me whole. 

I do it with clients, too, which is obviously even worse. They’ll be asking about target demographics and I’m already spitting out pricing options before they even hit the question mark at the end of their sentence. I can see them get this slight look on their face, like, "Did she really just interrupt me?" And I know how incredibly rude it comes across! I really do. It’s not that I don’t value what they’re saying or that I'm not listening, it’s just like my mouth is moving faster than my impulse control. The words are already out there in the air before I can tell myself to just bite my tongue, take a breath, and wait my turn. It makes me seem so impatient and scattered, and I just... I hate it, but I can't seem to stop doing it no matter how much I tell myself to just wait for people to finish speaking.
When you were a child, did teachers or adults often describe you as fidgety or unable to sit still?

You know, it’s funny you ask that, because when people talk about these kinds of issues, I feel like everyone immediately pictures that one kid in class who is just literally bouncing off the walls, right? Like, my cousin Matthew was exactly like that when we were growing up. He could not stay in his seat to save his life, he was always getting up to sharpen his pencil fifty times a day, tapping his feet, swinging his legs. 

But for me... no, not really. I don't actually remember anyone ever using the word "fidgety" to describe me, and I don't think my parents ever got told I couldn't stay in my chair. Like I was saying before about those old report cards my mom kept in that big binder, the notes were always, always about me talking out of turn or rushing through my spelling tests or having a desk that looked like a natural disaster. But physically sitting in the chair? I was actually pretty okay at that. 

I would sit there during, say, Mrs. Gable’s math lessons—she was my fourth-grade teacher, the one who used to make me stay inside during recess to clean out my desk—and I’d be in my seat the entire time. I wasn't running around the room or squirming out of my chair. I was just... mentally completely somewhere else. I'd be sitting perfectly still, but I'd be staring out the window at the playground, or I'd be meticulously peeling the paper wrapper off my crayons piece by piece, or drawing these elaborate little stars all over the margins of my notebook. So I was contained to my desk, it was just that my brain was doing all the running around, if that makes sense? 

So, physically unable to sit still? No, I don't think so. No one ever really complained about my physical energy levels. I was actually pretty good at staying put, as long as I had someone sitting next to me to whisper to or something to daydream about while the teacher was talking.
Do you still do a lot of impulsive things nowadays, like acting without thinking or making hasty decisions?

Um... you know, it’s funny, because after just telling you how I blurt things out and interrupt people, you’d probably think the answer would be a huge yes. But actually... no. Not at all, really. 

When it comes to actual actions, like making decisions or doing things, I am the complete opposite of impulsive. I am a massive, massive overthinker. Like, if we're talking about making hasty decisions? I literally cannot do that. I agonize over every little choice. 

In my job, you know, doing advertising sales, there’s a lot of pressure to make quick calls on deals or negotiate on the fly, but I never just jump into things. I always have to take a step back, look at the client history, review the numbers... I'm very cautious about what I actually commit to. 

And even in my personal life, oh my gosh, it’s actually a running joke with my friends. If we're trying to figure out where to go for dinner on a Friday night, I will spend forty-five minutes reading Yelp reviews, looking at the menus, checking the distance on Google Maps, cross-referencing everything before I can even suggest a place. I never just say, "Let's go here!" and walk in somewhere blindly. I just can't do it. 

And for bigger things? It's even worse. Like, I bought a new car last year, and I think I spent three entire months researching safety ratings, fuel efficiency, and depreciation values before I even allowed myself to set foot on a dealership lot. I had this massive color-coded spreadsheet with all the pros and cons of like, six different makes and models. I drove my boyfriend completely crazy because I just would not pull the trigger and make a choice. 

So, yeah, acting without thinking is definitely not me. It's weird, right? Because my mouth will just run off without my permission in a conversation, but if I actually have to take a physical action or make a choice, I freeze up and over-analyze every single possible outcome. So, no, I wouldn't say I do impulsive things at all. If anything, I take way, way too long to act.
Do you often feel physically restless, like you need to move or can’t stay seated?

You know, it’s interesting because I just said I wasn’t a fidgety kid, but as an adult... yeah, actually. Honestly, that specific thing is a huge part of what finally made me come in to see you. It’s become a real issue at work. 

In my agency, we have these massive, sprawling sales strategy meetings—they can go on for two, sometimes three hours at a time. We’re all packed into this big glass conference room, the VP of Sales is at the head of the table going over quarterly projections, and everyone else is just sitting there, perfectly fine, taking notes on their laptops. But me? I just cannot stay in my chair. 

After about forty-five minutes, I get this... this literal physical itch in my legs. I know I’m supposed to stay seated. It’s a formal meeting! But I just start making up these little excuses to get up. I’ll get up to refill my water bottle—and I’ll do it, like, three times in one meeting. Or I’ll pretend I need to grab a hard copy of the pitch deck we’re reviewing, just so I have an excuse to walk over to the printer and pace around it for a minute or two. 

And I know people notice. My coworker actually joked about it recently, asking if I was trying to get my daily steps in during the Q3 review. I laughed it off, but inside I was just so frustrated with myself. I just think, *Why can't I sit normally like a professional adult?* It’s just this overwhelming, restless urge to move, and half the time I’m sitting there just strategizing about when it’s socially acceptable for me to stand up again instead of actually listening to the revenue targets. So, yes, that feeling of needing to move is definitely there, and it's driving me a little crazy.
Do you often talk excessively or have trouble stopping yourself from talking?

Oh, wow, yes. Absolutely. I know I mentioned earlier about blurting things out and interrupting, but just the sheer volume of talking? Yeah, that is a massive thing for me. 

It’s actually really embarrassing, especially because in my line of work, obviously, you have to be a good communicator. You're selling, you're pitching, you have to be enthusiastic. But there is definitely a line between being an enthusiastic presenter and just holding the entire room hostage, and I cross it all the time. 

Like, when we do these big team pitches for new clients... I get so fired up. I’ll be presenting our angle, and I just get completely swept up in the campaign idea. I'll start explaining the core concept, and then I'll veer off into how we can adapt the messaging for different social platforms, and then I'll start detailing the exact kind of imagery we should use, and... it just snowballs. 

And the worst part is, while I'm doing it, I can actually hear myself going on way too long. It's almost like this weird out-of-body experience where a little voice in the back of my head is going, *Okay, you made the point, wrap it up, let someone else talk,* but my mouth just completely ignores it. I just can't seem to find a natural stopping point because every new thought feels so incredibly urgent and connected to the last one, and I'm terrified I'll forget it if I don't say it right that second. 

So I just keep going and going, and by the time I finally force myself to stop and actually take a breath, the energy in the room has totally shifted. I look around the table, and I can just tell that the rest of my team—like the creative director or the account manager—were literally just sitting there, completely stalled out, waiting for a chance to speak. You can see it in their body language, you know? They’ll have their hands raised slightly or their mouths half-open, just waiting for a gap in my monologue that never came. It makes me feel so guilty because I don't want to steamroll anyone, I really don't, but once I get going on an idea, I just... I don't know how to hit the brakes.
As a child, did you often leave your seat when you were expected to stay seated?

As a child? Um, actually, no. I really wasn't like that back then. I was always pretty good about staying at my desk. I mean, I went to this somewhat strict elementary school where they were super big on classroom rules, so you just didn't get up unless you raised your hand and asked for permission. I was way too much of a rule-follower to break that, so I'd just sit there. 

But... well, it’s exactly like I was literally just telling you a minute ago. It’s so funny you ask about leaving my seat specifically, because honestly, that exact behavior is what made me finally come in to see you in the first place! Like I was just saying about those long sales strategy meetings at the agency... I just keep getting up. 

I *know* I’m supposed to stay seated. I know exactly how it looks to the VP and the rest of the team. But I just can't do it. Even if it’s just to refill my water for the fourth time, or to go pace by the printer pretending I'm waiting for a revised contract to print out... I'm constantly leaving my chair. It's like I've completely lost the ability to just sit through a professional obligation like a normal adult, and it's so frustrating because I never had this issue when I was younger. So, yeah, not as a kid, but now? It's literally the main reason I'm sitting here talking to you today.
When you were a child, were teachers or adults ever concerned that you were too physically active or couldn't sit still?

Honestly, no, not at all. It’s so funny because when you hear about this kind of thing, you always picture the little boy bouncing off the walls, driving the teacher crazy, right? But that just wasn't me. I was the exact opposite of that kid. 

I remember in third grade, my teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was this older woman who wore these really loud, chunky necklaces and always smelled like peppermint—she actually used to tell my parents at parent-teacher conferences that I was a "model student" when it came to behavior. I mean, I would just sit there at my little desk with my hands folded. I was terrified of getting in trouble, honestly. If anyone even looked at me the wrong way, I'd probably cry. So I definitely wasn't running around the classroom or climbing on the playground equipment when we were supposed to be lining up. 

My parents never had any complaints from other adults, either. I did gymnastics for a few years—just the recreational kind, nothing serious, mostly because my best friend Sarah was doing it and I wanted to hang out with her—and even the coach there never said I was too energetic or anything. If anything, I was probably a little too timid. I'd stand in line for the balance beam and just kind of zone out, waiting for my turn, but I certainly wasn't doing cartwheels out of turn or, you know, being a disruption. 

So, yeah, it’s really strange to think about how much I struggle with feeling restless now, because back then, nobody ever had a single concern about my physical activity levels or my ability to sit still. It was just never on anyone's radar.
When you’re in situations where you have to stay seated, do you actually feel physically unable to remain in your seat, or is it mostly that your mind drifts off?

Oh, it's definitely not just my mind drifting. I mean, my mind does drift, obviously, but the feeling of needing to get up is so... physical. It's like this actual, tangible sensation in my body, almost like a buzzing or a tightness in my chest and my legs. 

It’s not just that I’m bored and thinking about what I’m going to have for lunch, it’s that my body is literally screaming at me to move. Like, I’ll be sitting in one of those endless budget review meetings—the ones where the finance guy is just droning on and on about Q3 projections and showing these incredibly dense spreadsheets—and I’ll start shifting my weight. Then I'll cross my legs, then uncross them, then I'll sort of lean forward, then lean back. And all the while, this feeling is just building and building until it feels like if I don't stand up right that second, I'm going to jump out of my skin. 

It’s almost painful, in a weird way. Not like a sharp pain, but just this overwhelming, unbearable discomfort. I try so hard to suppress it. I’ll dig my fingernails into my palms under the table, or I’ll bounce my heel, just trying to release some of that energy without actually getting up, but it never really works. It’s like trying to hold the lid on a pot of boiling water. Eventually, the pressure just gets to be too much, and I have to find some excuse—any excuse—to stand up, even if it's just for thirty seconds. So, yeah, it's very much a physical inability to just stay put, not just me zoning out.
Aside from the restlessness and talking, do you also often lose things or forget daily tasks?

Oh, gosh, yes. Losing things is practically my part-time job at this point. It’s actually become a running joke in the office, which is... well, it’s funny sometimes, but mostly it’s just incredibly stressful. I’m constantly, and I mean *constantly*, hunting for things I need for work. 

Just the other day, for example, I was supposed to be jumping on a quick sync call with a new client—this really important tech startup account we’re trying to land—and I could not find my headset anywhere. I tore my entire desk apart. I checked my bag, I checked the breakroom because I thought maybe I left it next to the coffee maker when I went to get my third cup of the morning, I even checked the bathroom. I was in a total panic, sweating, heart racing, thinking I was going to have to take the call on speakerphone in an open-plan office, which is obviously a nightmare. And you know where it was? It was draped over the back of my chair. I had literally just moved it five minutes before so I could sit down. 

And it’s not just the headset. It’s everything. Client one-pagers are the worst. I’ll print out these beautiful, full-color pitch decks, set them down "just for a second" while I grab a pen, and then poof—they’re gone. I’ll end up printing them three times before a meeting. My keys, too. I have this special bowl by the front door at my apartment that my sister bought me specifically so I’d stop losing my keys, but do I put them in the bowl? No. I’ll find them in the refrigerator next to the almond milk, or still in the lock on the outside of the door, which is honestly terrifying when you live in the city. 

And notebooks! Oh my god, the notebooks. I try to be organized, I really do. I buy these nice, expensive Moleskine notebooks, thinking, "This is it, this is the one I’ll keep track of." I’ll be taking notes during a creative brief, close it, go to the restroom, come back, and it’s like the notebook has vanished into thin air. I’ll be asking my coworkers, "Hey, did you see a black notebook? I was literally just using it ten minutes earlier." It makes me look so scattered and unprofessional. 

It’s just... it’s exhausting. It feels like I spend half my day just trying to locate the basic tools I need to do my job, and by the time I actually find them, I’m so flustered and behind schedule that I can’t even focus on the task itself. So, yeah, losing things is a huge, huge issue for me. It’s honestly one of the things that makes me feel the most out of control on a daily basis.
Do you currently have more trouble with inattention, or more trouble with hyperactivity and impulsivity?

Oh, wow. Um... that’s a really good question. I don't... I honestly don't know if I could pick one over the other? It’s almost like asking if I’d rather have a flat tire or a dead battery, you know? They both just completely derail my day, just in different ways. 

Because on the one hand, the spacing out and losing things—like I was just saying about the pitch decks and my headset—that makes me feel so incredibly incompetent. It’s like my brain is just a sieve. I’ll be sitting there trying to focus on a client’s needs, which is literally my entire job, to listen and respond to what they want so I can sell them the right ad space, and my mind is just completely on another planet. 

But then, on the other hand, the physical part... that awful, buzzing, crawling-out-of-my-skin feeling when I have to sit through one of those budget meetings? That is just physically exhausting. And trying to keep a lid on that restlessness takes so much of my mental energy that I end up not paying attention anyway! 

So, I guess they kind of feed into each other? Like, am I not paying attention because I’m so focused on not jumping out of my chair, or am I wanting to jump out of my chair because my brain can't focus on the spreadsheet? I really couldn't tell you which one is actually the bigger problem. My sister always tells me I’m equally all over the place in both ways. Like, just last weekend we were at brunch and I must have shifted in the booth a hundred times and dropped my napkin twice because I couldn't stop fidgeting, but I also completely forgot what I even ordered when the waiter came back. So... yeah, I really don't know. I guess I've never really thought about weighing them against each other like that. Is it normal to just not know which one is worse?
Before age 12, did you often have trouble staying seated when you were expected to remain in your seat?

Oh, definitely. I mean, I remember all of this starting way, way before high school. It was definitely happening long before I was twelve. If you look at my elementary school report cards—my mom actually kept all of them in this big plastic storage bin in her basement, and we were looking through them a couple of Thanksgivings ago—every single teacher basically wrote the exact same thing about me year after year. 

They always said I was a really bright kid, which was nice of them, I guess, but they always followed it up by saying that I constantly rushed through everything I did. And the talking out of turn was a huge issue. I just could never raise my hand and wait, I would just blurt things out, or I'd be turning around in my seat, or just getting up entirely to go talk to the kid at the desk behind me because I couldn't bear to just sit there quietly and wait for the next thing to happen. 

And the organization... or, well, the total lack of it. My teachers were always writing notes home because I constantly forgot my homework. Half the time I actually did the homework but I would just leave it on the kitchen table, or it would get completely swallowed up by my desk at school. My desk was a total disaster zone. It was just stuffed to the absolute brim with half-finished papers, squished folders, stray markers without the caps on... just a complete mess. Whenever we had to clean our desks out on Friday afternoons, it was like an archaeological dig just to find the bottom of it. I would pull out assignments from two months prior that I had just given up on halfway through. 

My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—or wait, maybe it was Mrs. Higgins? No, Higgins was fourth grade. Anyway, she was this very strict, tidy woman, and it drove her absolutely crazy that my space was always overflowing with all these abandoned worksheets and that I couldn't just stay in my chair like the other kids. So, yeah, this whole feeling of being rushed and scattered and not being able to just sit still and do what I was supposed to do... it’s been there since I was really little. It's funny how you don't realize it's a pattern until you look back at all those old teacher comments stacked up together, you know?
Do you also tend to fidget, tap your hands or feet, or otherwise feel like you need to move around a lot?

Oh, absolutely. Like I was just saying about the brunch with my sister, I am just constantly in motion. It's like I have this internal motor that just won't shut off, and the energy has to go somewhere. 

If I'm sitting at my desk—which I have to do a lot for my job, obviously, since I'm doing all these client calls and putting together proposals—my leg is just bouncing up and down non-stop. Like, a million miles a minute. I actually had a coworker, Dave, who sits in the desk cluster next to mine, and he actually stood up and looked over the partition once because the vibration from my foot tapping was shaking his monitors. I felt so incredibly bad, but I honestly didn't even realize I was doing it! 

And if it's not my feet, it's my hands. I am a serial pen clicker. I'll just sit there, click, click, click, click, while I'm trying to read an email. I've had people on Zoom calls actually ask me to mute myself because they could hear me playing with my pen or tapping my nails on the desk. I try to buy those pens with the twist tops now instead of the clicky ones, just to save everyone's sanity, but then I just end up twisting it back and forth until the pen falls apart in my hands. 

I just... I don't know, I just have this overwhelming urge to be doing *something* with my body. Even when I'm at home, trying to watch TV and unwind after a long day of sales pitches, I can't just sit on the couch. I have to be stretching, or getting up to check the fridge every ten minutes even though I'm not hungry, or picking at the seams on the throw pillows. It’s just this constant, restless energy. If I try to force myself to stay perfectly still, it almost physically hurts, like my muscles get all tight and my skin starts to feel like it's itching. So, yeah, the tapping and the fidgeting is definitely a constant thing for me.
Do your restlessness and need to move ever cause problems outside of work, like at home or in social settings?

Well, outside of work, I mean... I guess it definitely annoys my sister, like I mentioned with the whole brunch situation, and my boyfriend gets pretty frustrated when we're trying to just have a quiet night in. We'll be trying to watch a movie and I'm getting up a million times to check my phone in the kitchen, or I'm shaking the entire sofa because my leg is bouncing. He always ends up just putting his hand heavily on my knee to get me to stop, which is sweet of him to not yell at me, but it definitely makes me feel a bit guilty that I can't just relax with him. 

But honestly? Where it's really, really becoming a massive issue—and this is what's actually keeping me up at night and making me so incredibly anxious lately—is at work. It has actually started showing up in my performance reviews, which is terrifying. My manager sat me down for my quarterly evaluation last month, and we had this whole long conversation because my fidgeting and constant moving around is apparently starting to affect client trust. 

Which is just... it's so devastating to hear, because I care *so* much about doing good work. I really, really do. I put my heart into building these advertising campaigns and understanding what the clients need. But there was this one specific client complaint recently... oh my gosh, it was just awful. We were in a huge, important pitch meeting, and I guess I was doing the pen clicking thing, and shifting in my chair constantly, and kind of pacing a little too frantically when it was my turn to present. And the client actually reached out to my boss afterward and said I seemed "unprofessional" and "disengaged," like I wanted to be literally anywhere else but in that room with them. 

That just completely crushed me. It made me so worried that I could actually damage these accounts that I've worked so hard to build up over the last two years. Like, I'm trying my absolute best, and I'm super invested in their success, but my body just won't cooperate and sit still, and now it's actually threatening my livelihood and how people see me professionally. It's just so frustrating when your intentions are good but your physical restlessness makes people think you don't care, you know? So, yeah, it affects things at home a bit, but the work stuff... that's the part that really has me scared right now.
As a child, did your teachers or parents ever describe you as disruptive or causing trouble in class?

Well, I mean... I wouldn't say "disruptive" in the sense of being a bad kid, you know? Like, I was never the one pulling fire alarms or throwing things across the room or getting sent to the principal's office for being mean to other students. I was actually a pretty happy, friendly kid. My parents always said I was just very "spirited" or "bubbly." But... I guess if you mean disruptive in terms of just not being able to blend into the background and be quiet, then yeah, probably. 

Like I was saying earlier about Mrs. Higgins—or wait, no, Mrs. Gable, the third-grade teacher, I always get those two mixed up because their classrooms were right next to each other down that long hallway with the weird green carpet. Anyway, she definitely got frustrated with me. But it wasn't because I was trying to cause trouble! It was just... I just had so much to say, and I couldn't hold it in. If she asked a question about, I don't know, the water cycle, and I knew the answer, my hand would shoot up, but my mouth would just open at the exact same time. I couldn't do the whole "wait to be called on" thing. It was like there was a direct wire from my brain to my mouth that bypassed the "pause" button entirely.

And I know I talked to my neighbors a lot. I'd lean over to whisper to the girl next to me—her name was Sarah, we were obsessed with those little gel pens that smelled like fruit—and I'd just want to show her a doodle or ask what she brought for lunch, and before I knew it, the teacher would be saying my name in that very specific, warning tone. "Are we paying attention?" You know that tone. 

So my parents definitely got notes home about me being overly chatty or needing to work on my self-control during quiet reading time, because I'd be shifting around or sighing loudly because I was bored. But they never really framed it as me being a troublemaker. It was always more like, "She's very enthusiastic, but she needs to learn when it's appropriate to share." I tore my entire desk apart. I checked my bag, I checked the breakroom because I thought maybe I left it next to the coffee maker when I went to get my third cup of the morning, I even checked the bathroom. I was in a total panic, sweating, heart racing, thinking I was going to have to take the call on speakerphone in an open-plan office, which is obviously a nightmare. And you know where it was? It was draped over the back of my chair. I had literally just moved it five minutes before so I could sit down. 

And it’s not just the headset. It’s everything. Client one-pagers are the worst. I’ll print out these beautiful, full-color pitch decks, set them down "just for a second" while I grab a pen, and then poof—they’re gone. I’ll end up printing them three times before a meeting. My keys, too. I have this special bowl by the front door at my apartment that my sister bought me specifically so I’d stop losing my keys, but do I put them in the bowl? No. I’ll find them in the refrigerator next to the almond milk, or still in the lock on the outside of the door, which is honestly terrifying when you live in the city. 

And notebooks! Oh my god, the notebooks. I try to be organized, I really do. I buy these nice, expensive Moleskine notebooks, thinking, "This is it, this is the one I’ll keep track of." I’ll be taking notes during a creative brief, close it, go to the restroom, come back, and it’s like the notebook has vanished into thin air. I’ll be asking my coworkers, "Hey, did you see a black notebook? I was literally just using it ten minutes earlier." It makes me look so scattered and unprofessional. 

It’s just... it’s exhausting. It feels like I spend half my day just trying to locate the basic tools I need to do my job, and by the time I actually find them, I’m so flustered and behind schedule that I can’t even focus on the task itself. So, yeah, losing things is a huge, huge issue for me. It’s honestly one of the things that makes me feel the most out of control on a daily basis.

So, I guess they kind of feed into each other? Like, am I not paying attention because I’m so focused on not jumping out of my chair, or am I wanting to jump out of my chair because my brain can't focus on the spreadsheet? I really couldn't tell you which one is actually the bigger problem. My sister always tells me I’m equally all over the place in both ways. So... yeah, I really don't know. I guess I've never really thought about weighing them against each other like that. Is it normal to just not know which one is worse?
